<reason>PRO (Side B) won by seizing a single frame early—standards are the exam, "basic terms" are the post-approval regime—and holding it through every round. CON's case was sharp and disciplined, but its "trap" (new standards = not the same terms) was repeatedly defused by the pork/beef/poultry analogy: every meat takes a different exam yet lives under the same basic terms. CON's own concessions (no bans, tailored approval, harmonize later) let PRO plausibly argue CON was describing the motion, and PRO neutralized the ratchet with BSE/spinach recall examples. CON's best moment—naming three post-approval rules and distinguishing mandatory from voluntary labels—was met in PRO's closing by mapping them onto existing residue programs, process consistency, and illness surveillance, plus "previously frozen" and country-of-origin as mandatory beef disclosures. CON's final speech rebutted the drift point credibly, but by then CON's own A2 (criteria published at approval, met, then parity) had been turned into evidence that CON was specifying what "safety standards met" means rather than defeating the motion. PRO's opening clipping was a minor cost. Clear but competitive win for B.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B2.1–B2.8 turning CON's own examples (engineered salmon, irradiated food) and CON's "tailored pathway then harmonize" language into a concession of the motion, followed by B5.1–B5.4 folding CON's three special rules back into the existing meat regime and reading A4.3's exit criteria as "a safety standard with a clock."</best_rebuttal>
